analysis.one_liner: Extends bank anti-money-laundering rules to crypto exchanges, miners, wallet providers, and kiosks.
analysis.headline: Backed by 19 senators, the bill never got a committee or floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend the same anti-money-laundering rules that banks follow to the crypto world: exchanges, miners, wallet providers, and crypto ATM (kiosk) operators would have to verify customers, keep records, and report suspicious activity. It would also require Americans to report offshore crypto accounts holding more than $10,000, force kiosk operators to check ID and log counterparties, and direct Treasury to set controls on mixers and privacy coins that hide who is sending money. The bill never got a vote in committee or on the floor.
analysis.who_benefits: People targeted by crypto fraud benefit most: crypto ATMs have become a top channel for scams that drain seniors' savings, and the bill would force kiosk operators to verify customer IDs, record counterparty names and addresses, and update regulators on kiosk locations every 90 days. Victims of ransomware, drug trafficking, and sanctions evasion also benefit, since exchanges, miners, and wallet providers would have to file suspicious-activity reports and keep records that law enforcement can subpoena, and Treasury would gain tools against mixers and privacy coins used to hide stolen or laundered funds. Honest crypto businesses also gain a clearer rulebook and a field less tainted by illicit flows.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Scam victims, seniors, and law enforcement

how_it_helps.text: Makes digital asset providers and facilitators — including exchanges, miners, validators, and unhosted wallet providers — financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act, requiring them to keep records, file disclosures, and report suspicious activity to help detect money laundering and terrorist financing.

Requires crypto kiosk operators to verify each customer's government-issued ID, collect the name and address of each transaction counterparty, and report kiosk locations every 90 days — targeting the ATMs most used in scams against seniors — and directs the DEA to recommend ways to cut drug trafficking and money laundering through kiosks.
Directs Treasury to require controls on mixers, anonymity-enhanced coins, and funds that have been anonymized, closing tools used to hide ransom payments, drug proceeds, and stolen funds.

Requires U.S. persons to report offshore crypto accounts holding more than $10,000, the same disclosure banks and taxpayers already face for foreign accounts, and orders a FinCEN report on kiosk networks operating without registration.

analysis.who_pays: The crypto industry pays: exchanges, miners, validators, and wallet developers would carry Bank Secrecy Act compliance costs, registration duties, and exam risk, and kiosk operators would face ID-checking and location-reporting requirements. Crypto users also bear a cost — because even self-custody wallet providers and network participants would be treated as financial institutions, ordinary people transacting with their own wallets could see more of their activity collected and reported, a real loss of financial privacy. Some smaller participants, such as independent validators and kiosk operators, would likely shut down or move offshore rather than absorb the costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Crypto firms, wallet developers, kiosk operators, users' privacy

drawbacks.text: The bill sweeps far beyond exchanges: it would classify unhosted wallet providers, miners, validators, and other network participants as financial institutions, meaning software developers and Americans who simply hold their own crypto could face bank-style surveillance and reporting obligations on ordinary transactions.

Treasury would be directed to impose controls on mixers, privacy coins, and anonymized funds 'as specified by the Secretary,' which critics argue could effectively shut down privacy tools with lawful uses, since any transaction that touched an anonymized coin could carry risk obligations.

Compliance costs would fall hardest on small operators — independent validators and community crypto ATMs — pushing them out of the market or offshore, while large firms with existing compliance departments absorb the burden more easily.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine fraud and money-laundering problem in crypto, and the kiosk and offshore-reporting provisions are targeted, practical fixes with clear public benefits. But the bill's core move — turning every miner, validator, and wallet developer into a regulated financial institution — is badly designed for its purpose: it extends bank-style monitoring to people's own wallets and to network infrastructure rather than focusing on the services where illicit funds are actually cashed out. A narrower bill aimed at kiosks and exchanges likely would have drawn broader support and survived; the version introduced asked Congress to treat much of the open crypto network as a bank branch, which is a heavy privacy and feasibility cost that even sympathetic members were unwilling to sign onto.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee — three hearings, but never a committee vote or a floor vote — and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on July 27, 2023 with Senators Roger Marshall, Joe Manchin, and Lindsey Graham, a deliberately bipartisan pairing, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
The committee held hearings in October 2023, January 2024, and February 2024, but never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor.
Support stopped at 19 cosponsors — 16 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 Independent — and when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill was dead with no action beyond hearings.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Crypto companies, wallet developers, miners, kiosk operators, and privacy-coin users are better off because the bill died — they face no new reporting, registration, or ID-checking obligations. Americans who self-custody crypto also avoided new bank-style monitoring of their wallets, while scam victims and law enforcement gained nothing.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Wrote and introduced the bill to apply Bank Secrecy Act rules to digital assets, and built a bipartisan introduction with Marshall, Manchin, and Graham.

for.name: Roger Marshall, Joe Manchin, and Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Joined Warren at introduction, giving the bill Republican sponsorship from the first day.

for.name: 16 additional Democratic and 3 Republican/Independent senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, keeping the bill bipartisan but leaving it with support from fewer than one in five senators.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held three hearings on digital assets but never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Crypto industry groups, exchanges, and advocacy organizations (e.g., Coinbase, Blockchain Association, Coin Center)
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against the bill, arguing it would treat software developers and self-custody users as financial institutions and push the industry offshore.

against.name: The 81 senators who never cosponsored
against.what_they_did: Declined to add their names across 17 months, leaving the bill far short of the support needed to force floor action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill launched with two prominent Republican cosponsors (Marshall and Graham) alongside Warren, but support stayed at 19 senators — 16 Democrats, 2 Republicans, 1 Independent — and roughly three-quarters of senators of both parties never signed on.

industries.note: They would face full Bank Secrecy Act obligations — registration, record-keeping, suspicious-activity reporting, and exam risk. Many large exchanges already apply ID checks, so the incremental burden is compliance cost, but the rules would also extend to their network counterparties, raising monitoring duties across every transaction.

The bill targets kiosks directly: government-ID verification, logging every counterparty's name and address, updating kiosk locations with FinCEN every 90 days, and a DEA report on trafficking through kiosks. Kiosks are the top on-ramp for scams that hit seniors, so the industry's interest in avoiding these rules runs against consumers' interest in not being defrauded.

industries.industry: Crypto miners, validators, and self-custody wallet developers
industries.note: The bill would designate them as financial institutions, a category built for banks — miners and validators who never touch customer funds and free wallet software would face registration, reporting, and exam obligations. Their loss is partly the public's privacy loss too, since the rules would reach into Americans' self-custodied transactions.

industries.industry: Privacy technology: mixers and privacy coins
industries.note: Treasury would have to require financial institutions to impose controls on mixers, anonymity-enhanced coins, and any funds anonymized by them — effectively quarantining these tools. Treasury sees laundering vectors; users see financial privacy, and lawful uses would be caught along with criminal ones.
